name: DisplayName On Users Against The Denormalised OwnerDisplayName On Posts
description: A person's name lives in users.DisplayName. The posts table also carries an OwnerDisplayName column, but it is a denormalised leftover that is empty on almost every row, so reading it or filtering on it returns nothing for the great majority of posts. Whenever a question asks whose post something is, or names a person as the filter, resolve the person through users: join posts to users on posts.OwnerUserId = users.Id, or find the post first and look its owner up by Id. The same applies to comments and votes, each of which carries a UserId that points at users. Where a question asks what share of users something is true of, the denominator is the whole users table rather than the filtered rows, which a scalar subquery counting users supplies. Related phrasings: display name of the owner, name the user who, which user, whose display name, owner of the post.
sql: SELECT T1.DisplayName, T2.Title FROM users AS T1 INNER JOIN posts AS T2 ON T2.OwnerUserId = T1.Id WHERE T2.Score > 100

name: How Many Posts Created, Written, Or Made By A User Counts Through postHistory
description: A user is attached to a post by two different routes and the wording of the question decides which one applies. Ownership wording — the post owned by someone, the owner of a post, whose post it is — links users to posts directly on posts.OwnerUserId. Wording about the act of posting instead — a post made, written, created or used by someone, or work attributed to a person without any mention of owning it — runs through postHistory, joining users to postHistory on UserId and postHistory to posts on PostId, because postHistory records who performed each edit or creation event. Anything hanging off such a post, votes and comments among them, attaches on the same PostId once that join is in place. A question that wants the post identifier together with the person who created it can read PostId and UserId from postHistory alone, narrowing to the posts of interest with a subquery rather than joining the posts table for its own sake. Related phrasings: posted by, used by, made by, written by, created these posts, owner of the post.
sql: SELECT T3.Title, T2.CreationDate FROM users AS T1 INNER JOIN postHistory AS T2 ON T1.Id = T2.UserId INNER JOIN posts AS T3 ON T2.PostId = T3.Id WHERE T1.DisplayName = 'Chris'

name: A MAX Or MIN Subquery Against A Stored Column Of One Table
description: Reputation, Views, UpVotes, Age, Score and the other measures on users and posts are stored values, so the extreme one is a property of the table rather than something a ranking has to discover, and more than one row can hold it. Several users share the same view count and several posts share the same score, so asking which row is highest or lowest is asking for every row that reaches that value. Comparing the column against a scalar subquery over the same table, as in Views = (SELECT MAX(Views) FROM users), returns all of them; sorting and taking a single row silently drops the ties and answers a narrower question than the one asked. This applies when the measure being ranked sits on the same table as the answer and no other table is needed to work it out, which covers questions about the user with the highest reputation, the lowest view count, the oldest or youngest age, and the most valuable post. Related phrasings: which user has the highest, who has the lowest, the most number of views, the maximum reputation.
sql: SELECT Id, Text FROM comments WHERE Score = ( SELECT MAX(Score) FROM comments )

name: ORDER BY With LIMIT One Against A Measure Reached Through A Join Or A COUNT
description: When the quantity that decides the winner is not a stored column of the table being reported, the extreme has to be worked out by ranking rather than by comparison. Two situations create this. The measure may live on a table that has to be joined in, so the answer comes from one table while the ordering comes from another; the measure may instead be a count or a sum over a group, such as who wrote the most comments or which post drew the most answers, in which case the rows are grouped by the entity and ordered by the aggregate. In both the query orders the joined result and keeps the first row, and the ordering column may be one that is never projected. A scalar subquery is a poor fit here because the value being compared does not exist until the join or the grouping has happened. Where the ranked table already carries the identifier that is wanted, that identifier is read straight off the ranked row instead of being looked up through a further nested query. Related phrasings: the user who obtained the most, the post with the highest score, who posted the most comments, the badge of the user with the highest reputation.
sql: SELECT T1.WebsiteUrl FROM users AS T1 INNER JOIN votes AS T2 ON T1.Id = T2.UserId GROUP BY T1.Id ORDER BY COUNT(T2.Id) DESC LIMIT 1

name: A COUNT Of badges Or comments Rows Against A COUNT DISTINCT Of users
description: Asking how many users did something counts the records of the thing done rather than the people behind them. A row in badges is one award, a row in comments is one comment and a row in votes is one vote, each already carrying the UserId of the person responsible, so the count is taken over those rows and a person who appears twice contributes twice. Wrapping the user identifier in COUNT(DISTINCT) collapses that population into a headcount and answers a narrower question, returning a smaller number than the one wanted. Two consequences follow. Where the filter is a property of the activity itself, a badge name, an award year, a comment score, the users table adds nothing because the activity table already holds both the filter and the UserId, so the count runs over that one table with no join at all. Where the filter is a property of the person, a location or a reputation, the join to users exists only to apply that filter, and the count still runs over the activity rows rather than over the people. Related phrasings: how many users obtained, how many users are awarded, the total number of users who, how many users received.
sql: SELECT COUNT(T1.Id) FROM badges AS T1 INNER JOIN users AS T2 ON T1.UserId = T2.Id WHERE T2.Reputation > 5000
